This is going to be a long review.

I am by no means a survivalist extrordinaire. I wouldn't last 5 hours in Minecraft. But this game makes you feel like you can survive anything... until you run out of matches. 

For example, here is how I last died. 
I ran into the Trapper's Homestead, sprinting to get out of the freezing cold wind. I was looking for food; peaches, candy, anything I could get in my belly. I looked through the locker, the box under the bed, the first aid kit on the wall, but didn't find anything but an old can opener. Then I looked up, and I swear I heard a heavenly chorus, because sitting on a rack on the wall was something so much more valuble than a granola bar. As I took the old hunting rifle off the wall, I felt a sense of awe come over me. I looked at the nicks and dents and thought of all the stories that they contain, and how many more tales I would write with this pen of steel and wood. After looking around a little more, I decided to try my hand at cracking the safe I found next to the workbench. After several tries I finally got the code down, and lo and behold, inside was a box of 5 rifle shells. By now I was feeling like Rambo. I would not die to this cruel world! 
I survived by hunting the game that I saw in the clearing in front of the homestead that I had claimed as my home, and cooking the meat that I carved off their collapsed frames. I lived this way for about a week, until one very important setback to my otherwise flawless plan - I ran out of matches. But I wouldn't let that tiny detail stop me; I am the great VinyGroundhog! I will not succumb to the meager needs of hunger or cold! And thus my journey begain. I searched from house to house for those tiny life-sticks, but each and every one had been picked clean on a previous venture. I realized that there was only one place where I could find what I needed, one place that I had avoided like the plague. I was going to have to tackle the dam. 
As I walked into the dam, flare in hand, I looked for Fluffy the Terrible, Killer of Men and Crusher of Souls. I searched through the entire dam for this beast of legend, but nowhere was she to be found. Not able to contain my exitement, I set about looting the dam with a newfound vigor. I looked in the main room. No matches. I looked in the closet. No matches. I looked in the control room. Still, no matches. Soon I reached the conlusion that I was going to have to go downstairs. I walked down the first set of stairs, and as I rounded the corner, there was a nightmare standing in front of me. I stared at Fluffy, and she at me. We stood at a sort of stalemate for around thirty seconds. And then I ran like a coward. I made it up the stairs and Almost made it out when I was knocked down from behind. As I looked at those menacing jaws that I had fallen to so many times before, I knew that I was nearing my end. We struggled for what  seemed an eternity, and then I finally kicked the evil beast off of me, turning and sprinting through the door as fast as I could. By now it was night, and probably had been for a while. I struggled away from that horrible place, blood dripping down into the snow beneath. I looked around in my pack, and found nothing to treat my wounds. I walked along the train tracks, freezing, starving, dehydrated, and bleeding to death. I looked around and saw that I wasn't going to make it. But I refused. I would not die on the terms of a wolf, no matter that it sent me here. And then I thought of a way that I could stand up to the tyranny of the wolf. 
I sprinted to the logging area, and then I found the hill I was looking for. I started up the hill, made it a few yards, and subsequently fell off the hill and sprained my ankle. But I wouldn't let that stop me. I started back up the hill, limping this time, and made it farther, and farther, and farther without falling. And as I hobbled up the last few yards of the hill, freezing, starving, dehydrated, limping, and tired as anything, I saw the sun start to rise. I walked over to the edge of the hill, my vision rolling with every step, and sat down, leaning against a rock. And as my life reached its dusk, the world around me reached its dawn.

Words can't describe how much i love this game. So i'll just give you the lowdown of my favorite playthrough (Of dozens of great ones) 

Day 1: 
Plane crashed somewhere in the woods near a frozen pond and a hunting blind. I found (much to my joy) two granola bars and a bottle of water. Walking through the cold, i picked up a few sticks and some lichen just in case i needed to start a fire. After about 5 minutes of walking i found an old logging camp with three trailer houses. I scavenged a promising amount of food, got some matches, and even found an out ski jacket to wear over my sweater. Exhausted, i spent the night. 

Day 2: 
I wake up rested and thirsty as hell. I pop open a soda and head out. It's early morning and freezing, but i need to find a suitable place to bunker down, and those little trailers werent it. Following the snow covered trail through the woods, i pass a forest overpass. It's a long hike up in freezing weather and deep snow so i decide against, moving further down the trail. Right as i start to wonder if i had made the wrong choice, i hit a small frozen lake full of Ice-fishing huts. I dot through them and find a good set of stuff before i decide to bunker down in one for a little rest. After a few failed attempts i get the fire in the furnace going. I hear the wind picking up outside, but thinking nothing of it. I lay out my bedroll by the fire for a few hours sleep. 
I wake up to what i was sure to be my death. 
That light pickup of wind was a precursor to a blizzard. A bad one. The little hut was shaking and creaking in the storm, the opening (there was no door) let in frigid air and snow, putting out my fire and freezing me to the core. I gather my things in a panic. The storm is so fierce it's picking up snow that had settled on the ground, whiting out everything. I culdn't see five feet in front of me. Knowing staying in the hut would be my end, i blindly push into the storm, assumingly towards some camping lodges i saw when i first arrived. The wind cut straight through my clothes and the snow soaked my jeans, shoes and socks. My body trembled uncontrollably as heat was quite literally ripped from my body. After a few minutes the ice of the lake gave way to snow and i was sure i was close to salvation. I keep walking forward, waiting to see a beautiful log cabin any second.
Then i walk straight into a rock wall.
Panicking and wondering how the hell i got so turned around, i follow the wall, hoping beyond hope to find something to keep me safe until the blizzard gave way. I wasn't going to die yet, not here. I willed myself on, even when i felt so tired from the powerful wind i was ready to just drop. Eventually the rock wall gaveway to a some kind of house. Nearly collasping from relief, i get inside and fall asleep immediately, no energy left for anything else.

Day 3:
Apparentely this used to be a park ranger station. It was obviously abandoned in haste, as plenty of things were still left over. The blizzard is still raging, but im safe inside, with a decent supply to last me a few days. I cut up some furniture for wood with the hatchet i found in the closet and get the fireplace roaring. A get some snow quickly from outside and boil it for water, then i eat a hardy meal of beef jerky and a candy bar. I stay up a bit to assess my gear. Somehow i don't have hypothermia, but my pants looks a little worse for wear. I pathc them up with cloth then call it a day, i'm still exhausted from yesterday.

Days 5:
I'm stuck in the ranger hut for another full day. Finally, on Day 5 since my crash, the storm lets up to beautiful weather. I pack my things and head out, the Ranger station now depleted of useful things for me. I crunch along fresh now and a warm sun for a while, reminded of why i used to love skiing in New Mexico. After a while i find train tracks and few wrecked cars. It must of been carrying aid to somwhere becuase scattered amongst the snow i found antiseptic bottles, bandages, a bottle of painkillers and 3 flares. I rest for a bit and have a snack and a sip fo water, and move on. A little past 12ish i find what looks like an old hydrodam. Knowing there could be emergancy supplies and food inside, i make a beeline towards it and walk in, shutting the old iron door behind me.
The place is pitch black. I have to light one of my flares just to see. I look around for a bit, find a prybar and some other useful items including some workers old scarf (My new scarf now), and decide i'm going to spend the night here. 
Wrong decision.
As i preparing to set my bedroll down i hear a growl behind. Spinning around, the light from my flare provides me a eerie and terrifying look down the nearby hallway, where a wolf is looking right back at me, growling dangerously. Slowly, i begin to back out towards the door, and he charges me. I panic and throw the flare at him, which seems to scare him long enough for me to fly out the door and across the snow as fast as my damn legs could carry me. I run into the train tunnel and slow to a walk, trying to catch my breath, thank god the weather was still nice. I come out the other end just as the sun begins to set, and find myself in a massive ravine. 
After some hopping and skipping and a scary balancing act on a tree that feel across a 50 foot drop, i find a sheltered area behind a old train car and set up camp. I start a fire and give it enough wood to last the night. As i eat dinner i watch the sun set over the horizon. The light reflecting on far distant snow creates a beautiful allusion of fire, as if the horizon around me was burning briliantly. When it sets i am treated to freezing tempertures and a starry sky. I crawl into my bedroll and shut my eyes, hoping to god the weather treats me well.

Day 6:
I was lucky, i woke up to a light snow and nothing else. Hardly any wind. No wolves dragged me away last night so that was also a positive. Thanking my lucky stars i pack up and begin my journey west, to the coast. From there i planto keep heading down south to warmer weather. After traversing a particuarly large and rickety wooden train bridge (And almost falling to my death twice) i go through another tunnel and break out into the coastline. 
It was a beautiful sight. The sun glowing over all that sea ice. I would have watched forever if i wasnt freezing. Crawling down the mountain, i find another small trailer house (For the train unloading crew, i presume) and rest there. It felt nice to be inside again after almost 2 days in the wilderness. 

Day 7:
One week after my crash. Woo... Anyway, i woke up to howling this morning. More wolves. I headed further down the hill, another flare at the ready (I didnt even bother wielding an Axe, im not a swordsman). Sure enough, i run into one near the highway. It circles me before charging. I throw the flare at it and it runs away. Relieved, i walk over to pick up the flare when suddenly another wolf turns the corner, running after me full speed. I turned and ran like hell towards a cabin down the road. But right before i got to the door he grabbed my leg and i tried. In moments he was on top of me, ripping at the arm i threw up to defend my body. I hit him over and over until he finally let go, running away and barking angrily. Bleeding and hurt, i crawled into the cabin to treat my wounds, sure this was the end. I treated my wounds with antiseptic, bandged them up and took some painkillers. Then i slept.

I survived, and made my way to a cabin on a small island across the frozen bay. On my way, a white out struck. I couldn't see anything yet again. Walking slowly in hopes of not opening my wounds again. I pressed forward. Little did i know i had long past walked by the island, and was on thin ice. 
As the whiteout cleared, I looked up. It was as if every star in the universe was looking down at me. Somewhere in my mind, as the cold enveloped me, i wondered if anyone was out there...
Then I fell through the ice.

I shot a deer with my rifle, feisty things they are, for they do not die where they stand and run off for quite a distance.

This one was stubborn; he ran into the middle of a frozen lake to die.

Overjoyed was I, for it seemed like an easy place for me to gut the creature.

But there he was - the wolf. The damned beast, with his black mane and glaring eyes.
He sunk his teeth into the stag as it fell, as if it was his own.

The flame of hatred stirred inside me.
He so boldly dared to claim that which I had commanded to die, the life that was not his to take.

Unwavering I approached him upon the open field of ice.
Mine eyes were twin orbs of fury incarnate as I looked upon him devouring the essence which was rightfully mine.

The beast began to growl as I stepped ever closer, a fool does not know his own inadequacy.
Five meters were between us as I stopped.
He stood arched over the expired stag, growling at me as if [i]I[/i] was the intruder.

Perhaps once he had been the stalker of the forest, the one who the critters feared.

But no longer.

Into his forest hath arrived I, [i]the apex predator.[/i]

No thought, no emotion.
A swift motion summoned around him the gate of oblivion, which I knew to be the sights of my rifle.
Oh how foolish was he to not realize how he already stood inside.

A step of a black paw, the balancing movement of the tail, all for naught as death itself struck at my command.

The body of the black stalker lay down beside the stag, peaceful now in sleep eternal.

His flesh, like that of the stag, now existed only to sustain mine for a moment longer.
A quick rack of a rifle bolt echoes in the barren land. A worn knife is drawn from its shroud.
The grim work of harvest must now begin.

For there are no gods here.
Only Man.

I bought this game over a year ago, and I've seen it grow and change. It's gameplay mechanics have been altered completely, completely new areas have been added, and I see bug fixes almost instantly. The one thing that hasn't changed, however, is the fear it evokes. The devs completely nailed atmosphere. The music is eerie, the sound of your footsteps crunching on the snow urges you forward, and when it's pitch black and you wake up to a lone wolve's howl, well, it forces chills down your spine. You either press on, or you die. Fire is your best friend. Your attentiveness to the noises around you may save your life. The art leaves you looking forward to the sunrise the next morning, or paranoid as shadows dance over every shape around you. 

The gameplay is solid. The hud is minimal. The little details truly make it an immersive game. The voice acting when your character is over-encumbered or thirsty, the descriptions of all the items you pick up, and the first-aid system are all lovely examples. 

The Long Dark is personable. It's uniqueness in atmosphere and gameplay leaves you utterly alone and terrified and willing to fight. This is the most immersive survival game I have ever had the pleasure of playing, and I eagerly await story mode.

[b]Survival Mode — 10/10[/b]
If you're into sandbox and survival games, I definitely recommend this. You're looking at 200+ hours of slow, quiet, and atmospheric survival in a winter setting with a great ambient. You absolutely need to buy the DLC, as it adds a ton of new content. One of the best gaming experiences I've had in years.

[b]Wintermute — 4/10[/b]
The story mode, however, is a problem. Honestly, I wouldn't recommend it to either newcomers or experienced survivors. The main issue is that it's genuinely hard to cram survival gameplay into a standalone, often linear story mode where the events only span about 4-5 in-game days. A lot of the survival mechanics are designed for the long haul, so you simply don't get to fully enjoy all the elements of the game.

While the first few episodes could [i]barely[/i] be called "survival," by the end, it turns into a completely different genre. It's anything but The Long Dark. The final episode was really disappointing in this regard. During the entire 5th episode, I started exactly one fire, didn't melt snow for water even once, and didn't hunt a single animal... Even on the hardest difficulty, you just have a ton of loot, food, water, and so on. The game feels very linear, with zero hint of a proper open world. On top of that, there are a lot of dumb, cringe-inducing moments. [h1][b]The Long Dark is drowning in atmosphere. [i]No gimmicks.[/i] Just you and the wilderness. I've been following this game through it's lengthy beta and the wait has been worth it, the devs are steadily adding new content and developing the campaign mode, though the base survival is still my favorite. It's nuts how engaging this game makes trudging through the snow and rummaging through abandoned properties for hours on end. The subdued soundtrack and deep ambience mixed with simple but bright, and often eerily beautiful, graphics compliment the anxious slog toward your inevitable death. As a fellow game developer, this game gives me such conflicting emotions. I love it and hate it and wants more of it but also understands the current situation and the previous decisions. 

The difficulty in the beginning feels unforgiving, but it's where I find myself liking the most. Shivering in a snow storm not knowing where to go. You can feel the chill and despair in your bones, but just when you thought you are dead for sure, you find a small cabin. You go in, start a fire, boil some water, and your mind finally relaxes. You thought to yourself, maybe I can just make it through another day. That's one of the best feeling I've felt in a video game. 

But when you start to learn the map and mechanics, you find yourself acting purely with the goal of progression. Better gear, better clothes, the survival instinct is gone. Everything is predictable, you have the route and loot in mind, you go there, you get it, that's it. There is simply not enough variables or late game challenges that can put your knowledge to the test. Your hard earned lessons serve you only the dread of emptiness. You know not why to go on, where to go, everything just becomes a chore. 

It's such a shame. This game builds such a beautiful world and atmosphere, but it lacks some actual characters, story, mechanics and challenges. The wintermute story mode has a lackluster story and doesn't involve enough survival mechanics or player immersion. Tales from far territory is promising but requires you to go through much of the early stages that by the time you reach the new content, you are too burnt out to care. 

The slow pace of development and communication paints a picture of burnt out devs with low interest of improving this game. I'm a game dev myself and I totally get their frustration. This game had been through some rocky periods and significant goal shifts, probably due to financial and staff change problems. So I will not judge them too harshly, it's just unfortunate that it has come to this. 

So here are my suggestions to the development team. 
1. If you have abundant resources but got lost in the tunnel vision: Have a serious discussion about a total revamp of the current map, AI and loot system. Add more variables to the map to make shelters unpredictable, but utilize clues like roads and power lines to guide players to potential shelters. Add move-sets and behaviors to make the AI more unpredictable, maybe even give them the ability to break shelters so you can't just cabin cheese a bear with no risk or realism. Nerf the bottle necks like rifles and prolong each battle, make the hunts more difficult but rewarding. Decrease  and vary the punishment for a failed hunt. Give players more tools to approach a hunt like traps or melee options, not just QTEs. Make the crafting system more accessible and in-depth to increase the incentive to craft rather than looting for the better alternatives. There are many more ways to make this game more fun, especially for the late game. 
2. If you have few resources to continue development: Finish what you've started. It's too late to revamp the structure of the core mechanics. So at least just give the players what they've paid for, then move on to the next project with the knowledge and lessons you've learned from this game. 
3. if you don't have the resources to continue development at all: Try everything to gather resources. Communicate thoroughly and routinely with the players. Let us know where you are and what your obstacles are. Ask for help either in donation or just to spread the word for the game. Lay out new plans for monetization, new dlcs, new game modes, whatever to give us and investors hope. Give it a last ditch effort to turn it around.

I purchased The Long Dark about a year ago, clocked in roughly an hour and didn't play it again for a year.
Since I've redownloaded, I'm greeted with enough content to warrant a review.

Upon starting a new game on The Long Dark (albeit only Sandbox mode available) you are plonked into a world, barron with snow, a glorious vista sprawls out before you in every direction as far as you can see, you are equipped with a few warm clothes, and not much else, my first thought was to find a building that might have materiels for crafting. Within 5 minutes I had found said building, raided the entirety, decontructed all the wooden frames I needed for firewood, gathered food, found a hatchet, a prybar and a light source.
Happily I began to explore the darker areas of the building with my new found lightsource, whilst having my head stuck in a metal container suddenly a shrill wolf howl peirces the air, horrifyingly, I realise I am unarmed.
Carefully I tread now, I round a corner and my fears are realised, a lone wolf (takes a little while before noticing me) begins to charge at me, I 180 spin and haul my chilly little cheeks back towards the door, the wolf nipping on my heels.
I throw myself at the exit and dont stop to turn around, I sprint as far and as fast as I can cramming energy bars and grape sodas down my gullet as I marathon for escape.

The wolf growls die down, I am alive, however, during this encounter, and how engaging it was, I didnt pay any attention to where I was going, I find myself now, in the midst of a growing snow storm, with only 3 hours of daylight remaining, genuine panic sets in as my field of vision becomes smaller and smaller until I am able to see only a few feet in front of me in all directions, here i began to feel truly lost.
I drudge ever onwards, my food supplies are sparse, my water is disapated and I am dehydrated and freezing at an alarming rate, risk of hypthermia sets in, I pick a direction and travel, sure that my game is over and this harsh environment has claimed me.
I am exhausted, through the snow and wind I think I can see a rippling red flag so make ground for that.
Under the flag is a wooden hut, I push for sanctuary, my condition reaching a critical level as I turn the door handle.
Inside are two stoves, here I am able to keep warm, melt snow for hydration, cook tins of meat I found earlier after crudly opening them with a hunting knife, I brew a cup of coffee, set the fire to a few bars and get into bed and drift uneasily into sleep.

This was my Day One in "The Long Dark" a truly unique and genuinely quite nerve racking experience.
None of the above is dramatised.

While the graphics are shaded, I feel this adds to the gritty, post-apocolyptic environment "The Long Dark" is trying to promote, the mechanics and well thought out crafting system are just about balanced enough to keep you engaging in the environment to survive and explore, after one or two days, you begin to plan your 12 hours of available daylight, and prioritise expiditions based on what immediate resources are paramount to your survival, that is of course, before you find a reliable source of food, water, heat, and a warm place to lay down and get some rest.

Overall I am very pleased with my return to "The Long Dark", this title is showing alot of potential, and I look forward to future updates from this developer.

The mechanics of The Long Dark were, and still are, different from most survival games, anyone can tell you that. It’s grounded, pensive, it puts tension over action. Episode One was great, a personal story, of grief, of loss, of the old things, of things gone. I thought it was a great start, it worked great, it was quiet, and tense, full of discovery, of lives lived that are all too familiar. Abstract, a little, in a good way. Episode Two was amazing, getting back to the very beginning, to mystery lake, a new spin, new life to the rooms and roads I roamed back in the days when I didn’t know who I was. A bit strange with the whole bear thing, a little off putting with the mechanics and decisions, but still, it made sense. Jeremiah was great, and it was easy to suspend disbelief and get over some irritation here and there. The third had some tedium to it, but still, I played it through, I knew Pleasant Valley well and having new things to do there was good. Molly had an impactful, deep story. 

Wintermute first started to crack for me in Episode Four. I didn’t finish it in a few days like the others – I felt bored. Annoyance was too much to bear, and nothing to bear it for. Evil McEvil is not in any way compelling, and every other character repeatedly telling you what a bad guy he is and how evil, and also bad, and by the way, evil, is simply not good writing. The things you had to do felt more and more like pointless busywork, forced, unnatural, at times baffling with their dissonance and shallowness. Episode One had choices, a choice, at least, that felt like it mattered. Shame it was only once. Blackrock is a good region, but it wasn’t utilized nearly enough, and I barely even needed to eat, drink and sleep, since the cons let me go at full health, well fed, watered and energized every time. The gameplay was just wolf fight simulator. In the end, I just went on the easy difficulty and walked the whole story through to get it over with. Evil McEvil was a mediocre side villain at best, but him shrugging off everything felt forced in a game where tripping down a hill could make you fade into the long dark faster than you can say “oh no is that a bear”. Look, Evil McEvil is bad and he’s making a comeback next time, you better watch out! Hobbs was a better bad guy than this, and I talked to him for only five minutes. “This prison is well defended by the wilderness itself,” they said, “Escaped convicts asked to be taken back even in the summer”, they said, yet Evil McEvil and his goons are teleporting around the map like it’s vanilla Skyrim(while also being afraid to go outside because of the wolves).  

Episode Five is a sin. It’s a disfigurement on the face of a beautiful game.  It was so bad it felt almost hateful, like a job nobody wanted to do. Perhaps they shouldn’t have made it. A promise broken is better than a promise fulfilled in a genie way, making you regret ever wanting anything in the first place. Corridor locations throughout the whole story with wolves dropped around the bends and in the corners, “because it’s long dark”. Survival part of the game crumbling into dust. If you want to make a walking simulator with a story, go make it elsewhere. The big story reveals seem to have been pulled out of somebody non-buisness end, flat and boring “everybody went insane by the way”. Astrid chapters were lazy. Mackenzie’s were disgusting. Snarky millennial writing throughout, everybody dropping sarcastic one-liners about the mechanics with disdain.  Disrespecting your own medium to the point of sticking fourth wall nudges all over the place. Episode one Mackenzie was a divorced father, who never had recovered from the loss of his only child, going on because there’s nothing left but to go on. Episode five Mackenzie owns a funko pop collection, talks like he’s trying to earn twitter points and is fully aware he’s there just because of the plot. Him catching a bullet with the hard case and being like, hey that’s why I was carrying it I guess, left whatever drama they tried to do afterwards stillborn. Evil McEvil is still evil. Look at him doing evil things. Embarrassing to witness. The mines add insult to injury – it was clearly an attempt to showcase the sequel co-op mechanics but it’s not an ad, it’s a smear campaign. Never have I been so sure I don’t want a co-op long dark than after playing the mines. Friendslop, banter, more snarky one-liners and characters getting whiny about being in a survival game. Again, if you don’t like making it, quit. Snarky McSmart and Old McSmart with the science gibberish that doesn’t add up. The shotgun. I half expected the end to be a first person shooter when I got it. Why not an AK-47? Or is that going to be in a DLC now. Shame on you. The train is stupid and a waste of time. Linear stealth with mechanics worse than in games from the 90s is stupid and a waste of time. TLD is not that kind of game, and if you wanted to do a different one, you should’ve. The end is forced, pointless, frustrating, it’s an idiot plot based entirely on “we could’ve killed Evil McEvil twenty times but we forgot, bad ending now I guess”. You don’t get to decide. 

Episode Five is like marriage ending fight, sending over a decade we’ve had together down the drain with no hope to get in back. It can’t be fixed. An apology won’t do. I want to know why, but also I don’t, and also I already do. I wished for a different heartbreak with Episode Five. Thanks for everything. Goodbye. Have a nice life.

I bought The Long Dark sort of on a whim. I had some money left over during the Steam summer sale after I had bought all the games I had planned to buy. After looking at the screenshots and reading some reviews I decided to try the game.

I've played survival games before, but none really left an impact on me as I was playing and after I had "finished" like this game did.

I started the game clueless, on a hill looking over a few trailers. I figured out the mechanics pretty quick, and was instantly impressed by the art style. unfortunately, I only made it ~30 minutes before I died, but I leraned from that first time.

This game is made in Unity (the same engine as angry birds 2), but looks absolutely stunning because of the fantastic art direction. Everything in the game looks like it belongs in a watercolor painting. It is one of my favorite games ever, visually, even including 8th generation games. At night, the landscape is bathed in darkness, and in the daytime it's bright and vibrant. In the afternoon, the sky is bright red and orange, and looks magnificent. In blizzards, you can barely see 5 feet in front of you and looks and sounds menacing.

The sound design in this game is also amazing. Aside from the often foreboding ambient music, you'll get used to only the desolate sounds of your own footsteps, aside from when you hear the growl of a wolf or the grunt of a bear.

The gameplay is very good, and fairly challenging. You have to make sure you have enough supplies to survive, which means venturing out, where you could be killed by wolves, bears, or the cold. You're always making calculated risks, and if you make them well, you'll survive, if not, you'll end up as one of the frozen corpses you find in the snow. It's also very slow and tense. When the sun was going to set in 3 hours and there were wolves all around me, but I was overburdened, tired, and cold, every footstep towards safety seemed to take an eternity. But then, that's the point.

I personally never encountered any bugs or glitches, aside from some VERY small graphical glitches. My experience with this game overall was phenomenal, but unfortunately cut short by a bad decision(shooting a bear in the ass ,which is why I put "finished" in quatations).

Overall, this is a game I would highly reccomend to just about anyone, unless you're not a fan of planning and management. The quiet intensity and beauty of The Long Dark make it a very memorable and exciting experince to play. (just don't shoot a bear in the ass , trust me)

This doesn't apply to the whole game-just episode 5. 

I rarely leave reviews, but I couldn't stay silent here. Episode 5 is awful. You just walk from one spot to another. The point of surviving or scavenging is gone. The dialogue is long and boring. You can't skip it. I've already read everything they say and still have to listen for another 30 seconds while they finish. I had a strong playthrough once. I made it to around day twenty, having gone through three of the available areas at the time, and I was doing good, but it was not long lived. My resources were dwindling as I made my way to the last supplied area at the top of a mountain, a lone radio station secluded from the rest of the map. It was starting to get dark, and my body temperture was dropping fast, so I lit my lantern and started to run. Out in the darkness I heard a howl, followed by another that seemed much closer. I put away my lantern and took out my rifle, aiming it towards the origin of the noise. I heard a growl about ten feet away, so I fired a shot. A whimper pierced the whirring of the cold winter air around me, then silence. Not taking any chances, I lit a flare to see what was around me. Five feet in front of me was a pair of wolves, one was bleeding profusely from his gunshot wound, while the other was preparing to leap onto its would be prey. Being only fifty feet from the radio station, I decided to make a break for it. I threw the flare at the wolves face and sprinted away. The rapid stomping of my feet began to slow as my stamina quickly depleted. No heat for miles takes a toll on the body, and I was slowly dying just feet from my salvation. I heard fast taps on the ground behind me as the wolves closed in for the attack. I was almost there, just a few more steps until I could get into the station and shut the door, then the wolf pounced. I was on the ground, hacking it apart with my axe as it took gnawed on my half frozen flesh. It was a bite away from ending my long journey, when I took one last swing with my hatchet and killed it. I got up and limped toward the door, just barely making it into the station before the other wolf had a chance at killing me. I made it. Inside was much needed health supplies, and much needed food. I started a fire and cooked some venison, all the while warming my body temperture to its original state. I then went to sleep in the nearby cot, gaining health, yet also gaining thirst and hunger. My supplies were low, maybe a few energy bars and a few cans of soda, definitely not enough to last a voyage out into the unknown, so I decided that my journey had come to an end. I quit the game and said goodbye, for I knew that if I continued I would surely perish. I couldn't watch my character die, after all we had been through, he didn't deserve to fade into the long dark. So I let him live in that save, untouched and undying, until I decide that it's time for his journey to come to a close. Until that moment, I will always cherish my adventure I had, and I hope that one day I will have the courage to once more venture out into the unknown, making my way through the barren landscape, and surviving the long dark.

Got this game a few years ago when it was in early access. Played it on and off during that time for a total of about 12 hours and I wasn't really sure how I felt about the game. It can be very slow and "boring". However, something I have come to appreciate after picking it up again is how many decisions the player is subconsciously making and how these decisions, despite their ubiquity, never take over the gameplay experience. For example, the main survival loop revolves around keeping 4 meters topped off: temperature, fatigue, thirst, and hunger. The most efficient place to recover temperature is indoors, but the only place to get food is outdoors, so the player can never stay in one location for too long unless they've planned for it by stocking up food. When the player goes out to get food, temperature starts to drop, meaning that the player wants to spend as little time outside as possible and get the most food, so inevitably they will sprint around. But sprinting depletes fatigue very quickly, meaning a person might need to go to sleep earlier to top off fatigue, which will mean that you will wake up at night, which is a time when it is even colder outside so you lose temperature even faster so you have less time to get food but if you're hungry it might be a better idea to hunt at night because if a blizzard rolled in later in the day then you'd lose even more temperature and probably be blind. And you're constantly going through these long strings of "what-if" scenarios while taking your peaceful morning stroll to check all your snares.

Basically, you simultaneously get an intense experience where you could potentially end up freezing and/or starving to death, mixed with a peaceful "walking simulator" that underscores the tranquility of nature. This duality provides evolving and unique gameplay that remains engaging if you are in the right mindset.
No lie, I have over 900 hours logged on this game. I've had the game for 6 years, been here through countless updates and it keeps getting better.

Survival games are 'trending' With games like 'Rust' and '7 Days to Die' being amongst the current popular titles.
I purchased The Long Dark as it promised a more realistic approach to this genre.
I have very mixed views on the realism of the game, on one hand it provides an excellent sense of urgency as you struggle to find the basics to provide warmth (the cold being the biggest threat). You also face the challenges of finding food, medicines, and other basic supplies.

I made the mistake of fishing too late one evening, and realised it was already dark outside. I had (stupidly) left my lantern and firewood at my camp to lighten my pack weight. While trying to guess which way was home I got turned around in the dark and subsequently died of cold and tired exhaustion while stumbling around looking for shelter.... This was excellent! I loved how one simple mistake could have such serious consequences.

However... I dislike some of the limitations in the game, you cannot interact with all of your surroundings, you cannot climb or jump so even small rocks or branches can be an impassable obstacle, you cannot chop wood on scavenge bits, you find lots of corpses but cannot remove their clothing to replace your own, you find lots of blankets and material but you cannot use those to warm yourself they can only be broken down into cloth to repair or craft items. The crafting is also very very basic. 
Basically, I found myself frustrated and thinking 'why cant I do ........, it is common sense' 

From what I have played so far, I can happily say it can be a difficult game with an unforgiving learning curve that offers hours of interesting and challenging game play. BUT it isnt without its frustrating little flaws.

Great little game, I bought it on sale and am very happy, however I wouldnt have been as pleased if I had paid full price.
